title: Tele-Cranio: a CT-free AI solution for remote diagnosis and planning of craniomaxillofacial deformities
desc: Computed tomography (CT) is central to craniomaxillofacial (CMF) deformity care, yet dependence on in-hospital imaging constrains remote preoperative assessment and outcome visualization, and repeated imaging can increase radiation and access burdens, particularly for children. We developed Tele-Cranio, a telemedicine-oriented artificial intelligence framework that uses mobile-acquired 2D facial photographs to reconstruct 3D facial morphology, estimate corresponding skeletal morphology and support postoperative facial simulation conditioned on surgeon-defined skeletal plans. Tele-Cranio was developed using 539 paired multimodal samples comprising 2D facial photographs, 3D facial scans and CT-derived skeletal models from individuals aged 3–60 years, including 334 patients with CMF deformities across malocclusion, cleft lip with/without palate, hemifacial microsomia and rare anomalies. Its core model, the Bidirectional Craniomaxillofacial Model-Deformity, learns a shared anatomical representation linking facial soft tissue and skeletal structures across normal and pathological morphology. For remote assessment, Tele-Cranio converts facial photographs into 3D facial surfaces and then infers 3D patient-specific skeletal geometry. For simulation, it generates individualized 3D postoperative facial previews after clinicians complete skeletal planning using standard clinical tools. Validated across heterogeneous CMF subgroups, Tele-Cranio provides an interpretable CT-free layer for remote triage, pre-CT consultation, radiation-free follow-up and surgeon–patient communication, while complementing rather than replacing CT-based definitive diagnosis and operative planning.

title: Artificial intelligence and triple negative breast cancer: can pathomics help oncologists?
desc: [Frontiers in oncology] Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is an aggressive and heterogeneous subtype of breast cancer with limited targeted therapies and poor prognosis. Recent advances in digital pathology and artificial intelligence (AI) are transforming traditional, qualitative histopathology into quantitative, data-driven analysis. Within computational pathology, pathomics (the extraction of handcrafted, high-dimensional features from digitized histological images) and deep learning (DL)-based whole-slide image analysis have been investigated for the prediction of molecular subtypes, biomarker expression, tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, and treatment response in TNBC. AI models, including DL and multimodal systems integrating histopathology, omics, and clinical data, are being explored for patient stratification, risk assessment, and therapy personalization, encompassing chemotherapy, immunotherapy, PARP inhibitors, and antibody-drug conjugates. By linking spatial tissue architecture with molecular profiles, these approaches may provide new insights into tumor biology and the tumor microenvironment. Most TNBC-specific studies are retrospective, small or single-center, few have been externally validated and, to our knowledge, none has yet demonstrated clinical utility in prospective trials; prediction of biomarkers such as PD-L1 or homologous recombination deficiency from hematoxylin and eosin slides remains investigational and cannot replace validated testing. Despite these challenges, AI-assisted computational pathology is a promising decision-support tool, which complements and does not replace pathologists and oncologists, for enhancing diagnosis, prognosis, and therapeutic decision-making in TNBC.

title: Mind2Act World: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Embodied Mind, Physical Action, and Mind-Action Composition in Robotic Manipulation
desc: Embodied intelligence aims to let robots perform complex physical tasks with human-like adaptability and reliability, which requires three complementary capabilities: history-based cognitive reasoning, precise and timely physical execution, and the composition of reasoning and execution through environmental feedback. Yet existing benchmarks either evaluate reasoning and execution within the same tasks or assess them separately without their composition, so they reveal little about whether a failure comes from reasoning, execution, or their composition. We introduce Mind2Act World, a diagnostic benchmark of 30 simulated manipulation tasks from five real-world application domains. Each task has three difficulty levels and two scene settings (Clean and Random), yielding 180 configurations. The tasks form three views: Mind tests decisions based on past observations, Act tests precise and timely execution, and Mind2Act combines both in closed-loop tasks where action outcomes guide later decisions. Comparing the three views shows whether a system lacks a capability or fails to compose capabilities it already has. A diagnosis harness further attributes the failed episodes of three representative systems to Mind, Act, or their composition and summarizes each system in a profile card. Our evaluation of multimodal agents, vision-language-action models (VLAs), and world-action models (WAMs) shows that competence in a single view does not carry over to Mind2Act tasks. Even the strongest agent succeeds in 52.7% of Mind and 39.0% of Act episodes but in only 12.0% of Mind2Act episodes. The strongest agent retains task state but struggles with sustained contact, whereas end-to-end policies execute practiced motions but retain little task state. These findings point to composing reasoning and execution through environmental feedback as the main open problem.

title: The ITE-Transformer: A pre-trained foundation model for predicting individualized treatment effects from electronic health records
desc: Transformer-based foundation models have shown strong potential for modeling longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs), yet existing models focus primarily on risk prediction rather than treatment effect estimation, which limits evidence generation. Here, we introduce the ITE-Transformer, a transformer-based framework that combines self-supervised representation learning from longitudinal patient trajectories with doubly robust causal machine learning for predicting individualized treatment effects (ITEs). As a result, our ITE-Transformer allows to study counterfactual questions of how an individual patient's outcome may differ under alternative treatment strategies. The ITE-Transformer learns temporally contextualized representations of patients' diagnosis and medication histories and subsequently uses these representations to predict treatment assignment, treatment-specific outcome risks, and patient-specific ITEs. The ITE-Transformer is trained using structured EHR data from ~350,000 participants in the All of Us Research Program and evaluated in two clinically different comparative-effectiveness tasks: (i) GLP-1 receptor agonists versus DPP-4 inhibitors among patients with type 2 diabetes, with major adverse cardiovascular events as the outcome, and (ii) immunotherapy versus chemotherapy in a pan-cancer cohort, with all-cause mortality as the outcome. Across both applications, the ITE-Transformer improves the discrimination and calibration of treatment assignment and outcome models compared with existing tabular machine learning approaches and an otherwise identical transformer trained without self-supervised pre-training. The ITE-Transformer further identifies substantial heterogeneity in predicted ITEs and yields interpretable patterns of treatment response associated with patients' diagnoses, medication histories, and comorbidities. Together, our work demonstrates how clinical foundation models can be developed for analyzing heterogeneity in treatment effects and thus support real-world evidence generation.

title: Modelling Phenotypic Assay Noise for Multivariable Biomarker Discovery using Deep Neural Networks
desc: Accurately predicting cancer drug response remains a major challenge in precision oncology. Although some therapies are guided by clinically-approved biomarkers, these markers often yield limited predictive value and are unavailable for many drugs. Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning approaches trained on large-scale cancer cell line pharmacogenomic screens offer a promising route to more comprehensive response prediction, yet they generally assume that phenotypic readouts are measured without error. This assumption is problematic because viability-based drug response assays are inherently noisy, potentially causing models to learn experimental artefacts rather than biologically meaningful determinants of sensitivity. Here, we show that phenotypic measurement noise is present in four widely used cancer cell line screening datasets and introduce Deep Concordance Index Networks (DeepCINET), a deep learning framework that explicitly accounts for this noise. Across datasets, incorporating this noise-aware ranking strategy improves generalization across experimental conditions and to previously unseen samples. DeepCINET outperforms baseline models in multiple settings, with particularly notable gains in prioritizing the most drug-sensitive cell lines. Together, these results establish phenotypic assay noise as a critical and previously overlooked source of error in drug response modelling and provide a principled framework for noise-aware multivariable biomarker discovery.

title: Learning to Defer under Expert Drift
desc: The learning to defer (L2D) framework enables safety in machine learning and AI systems by allocating difficult or critical decisions to a human expert. However, most prior work on L2D assumes fixed expert reliability, overlooking temporal fluctuations in human performance due to factors such as fatigue and cognitive biases. Humans commonly exhibit such substantial, systematic performance shifts across a wide range of domains, from high-stakes settings such as radiology, aviation, and judicial decision-making, to everyday tasks such as crowdsourced image annotation. We propose Expert-Drift-Adapted Learning-to-Defer (EDA-L2D), a novel expert-aware L2D framework that explicitly models these temporal shifts by conditioning the deferral head on recent histories of expert outcomes via a sequence model. This history-aware approach enables adaptive deferral policies that anticipate reliability fluctuations and better allocate decisions between human and machine over time. We provide comprehensive experiments across three diverse tasks -- image classification, medical diagnosis, and hate speech detection -- including generalization analyses under realistic deferral conditions and irregular shifts in expert reliability. Our results show that EDA-L2D adapts more effectively than prior L2D methods to diverse temporal patterns of expert reliability, resulting in improved system performance and more effective deferral decisions. Code is available at https://github.com/ZiyaoMou/L2D-Expert-Drift.

Virtual atrial fibrillation dynamics reflect clinical outcomes after catheter ablation
desc: Chamber-wide assessment of restitution dynamics is not feasible in vivo during atrial fibrillation (AF) ablation. We reconstructed left-atrial digital twins from high-density (HD) bipolar electroanatomical maps in 323 patients, computed node-level restitution steepness (maximal restitution slope [Smax]; >0.4 million nodes), and induced virtual AF with standardized ramp pacing to classify sustainability (sustained ≥16 s vs non-sustained <16 s), excluding 32 cases with extensive low-voltage substrate and depressed mean Smax. We found that clustering of HD restitution profiles identifies four restitution patterns that stratify clinical atrial arrhythmia recurrence, with the Overall-Low pattern (aHR, 0.37) and the Average-Homogeneous pattern (aHR, 0.59) each showing lower risk than the Overall-High pattern. Furthermore, non-sustained virtual AF independently predicted lower recurrence (aHR: 0.27). Adding restitution pattern and sustainability to clinical covariates improved discrimination (ΔHarrell’s C-index: 0.050), and the combined digital-twin model remained incremental after adjustment for low-voltage area burden, supporting digital-twin outputs as complementary functional descriptors for risk stratification after pulmonary vein isolation.

title: Application of artificial intelligence in the diagnosis and treatment of thyroid cancer.
desc: [Frontiers in endocrinology] Thyroid cancer is one of the most common endocrine malignancies, and its rising incidence has increased the demand for more accurate and efficient diagnostic and management strategies. Current clinical management mainly relies on ultrasonography, fine-needle aspiration (FNA), surgery, radioactive iodine therapy, thyroid-stimulating hormone suppression, and systemic treatment in selected advanced cases. However, substantial interobserver variability, indeterminate cytology, and heterogeneity in tumor behavior still complicate diagnosis and risk stratification. In thyroid cancer, AI(Artificial intelligence) -assisted models have been applied to ultrasound, CT, MRI, cytology, histopathology, and genomic data, with promising performance in distinguishing benign from malignant nodules, predicting lymph node metastasis and key mutations, and supporting individualized management. This review critically synthesizes evidence across these applications, focusing on study design, validation strategies, generalizability, and clinical relevance. It also examines explainable AI, emerging foundation models, and regulatory and implementation challenges. Although many models report high diagnostic or predictive performance, these results alone do not establish improvements in clinical decision-making or patient outcomes. Prospective clinical validation, cost-effectiveness assessment, and evaluation of integration into clinical workflows are needed to determine whether AI provides meaningful benefits over standard care.

title: CurvDelta: Low-Curvature Delta Modeling For Surgical Learning and Unlearning
desc: A central challenge in adapting large language models (LLMs) is capability preservation: an adaptation can achieve its target while degrading general capabilities. We introduce CurvDelta, a scalable framework that incorporates the preservation constraint into the parameterization of the model update. By analyzing the local geometry of the preservation constraint around the pre-adaptation model, CurvDelta constructs a low-curvature space in which parameter updates leave the preservation loss nearly invariant. We make its construction practical for LLMs through Kronecker-factored approximate curvature (K-FAC) and a factorized projection. We also introduce CurvLoRA, a low-rank variant within the same preservation geometry, designed for more efficient adaptation. Both methods apply to preservation-constrained adaptation tasks such as capability learning and selective unlearning. We evaluate our methods on mathematical reasoning, code generation, and knowledge unlearning. For mathematical reasoning and code generation, our approaches achieve competitive downstream performance while better preserving general capabilities, offering a favorable acquisition--retention trade-off relative to the baselines. For knowledge unlearning, our main results on TOFU and MUSE show a better balance between targeted forgetting and knowledge retention than the baselines, with retention performance close to the from-scratch retraining reference.

title: Patient-Expressed Needs, Burdens and Barriers in Taiwanese Online Health Discussions: A Taiwan-Contextualized Friction Framework Applied With Large Language Model-Based Social Listening
desc: Background: Patients' difficulties with illness and care (not understanding a result, distress, daily restrictions, not knowing where to go, family strain) may not surface in clinical encounters or records. title: NeuroSim: a clinically informed multi-disorder EEG simulator with personalized pattern injection and AI-driven neurological modeling
desc: Deep learning for electroencephalography (EEG) based neurodiagnostics is constrained by the limited availability of labeled clinical recordings. Datasets covering Alzheimers disease (AD), Parkinsons disease (PD), schizophrenia (SCZ), epilepsy (EPI), and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) are scarce, demographically narrow, and heterogeneous across acquisition sites, while privacy requirements restrict data sharing. Existing EEG simulators typically address a single disorder or trade biological interpretability for statistical fidelity. This study presents NeuroSim, a simulation framework that generates synthetic multichannel EEG with user-controlled injection of disease-specific patterns across five disorders and multiple severity levels. A physiologically motivated baseline generator produces band-limited rhythms, event-related potentials, artifacts, and hierarchical subject-level and trial-level variability. Disease patterns are introduced through region-specific and severity-specific spectral modulation that encodes established biomarkers, including posterior alpha suppression in AD, motor beta enhancement in PD, and spike-wave discharges in EPI. An interactive interface exposes montage, sampling rate, duration, artifacts, stimuli, affected regions, and severity, and exports signals with reproducible metadata. The simulated signals reproduced the expected biomarker directionality under spectral, topographic, and multivariate statistical analysis. A convolutional-attention classifier trained on simulated data reached 95.3 to 96.8 percent hold-out accuracy, and post hoc explainability analyses produced class-separable embeddings with attributions concentrated on pathophysiologically expected electrodes. Application of the analysis pipeline to recordings from the Temple University Hospital EEG Corpus confirmed compatibility with heterogeneous clinical data. In subject-level augmentation experiments on real clinical EEG, supplementing real training data with NeuroSim samples increased classification accuracy from 91.6 to 94.5 percent for AD versus healthy controls and from 90.9 to 94.0 percent for PD versus healthy controls, exceeding the improvement obtained with conventional signal-level augmentation. NeuroSim is released as open-source software to support augmentation, benchmarking, and explainable artificial intelligence in neurological diagnostics.

title: Bayesian optimization on amortized search space
desc: In real-world black-box optimization problems, a mechanistic simulator is often available that approximately predicts the behavior of the system as a function of the parameters being optimized. Here, we show how an amortized inverse map of such a simulator can be used in Bayesian optimization to restrict the search space while using a Gaussian process kernel that is aware of the original problem geometry. This allows for efficiently leveraging the low intrinsic dimensionality of the optimization problem. We characterize its approximation bias and information gain, and derive an intrinsic-dimension-dependent regret rate under additional geometric and Gaussian Process assumptions. We illustrate the method with an application to drug dosing personalization in Parkinson's disease. We use, as a simulator, a pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) model of a drug, a mechanistic model calibrated on population data with quantified parameter uncertainty. A dosing neural network is trained offline against the model, amortizing the map from patient PK/PD parameters to the regimen predicted to be optimal, and online Bayesian optimization then searches over this learned, low-dimensional representation rather than over raw dosages. Numerical simulations demonstrate the improved performance of our method in this application, as well as under simulator misspecification.

Epidemiology-informed graph neural networks for predicting and interpreting transmissible hospital-acquired infections
desc: Transmissible hospital-acquired infections (HAIs) arise from complex, time-varying interactions among patients, healthcare workers, and clinical environments. Although data-driven approaches like graph neural networks (GNNs) effectively model these contacts, they often function as black boxes that overlook established epidemiological principles, limiting interpretability and clinical trust. Inspired by physics-informed neural networks, we propose an epidemiology-informed GNN (EIGNN) framework for patient-level state transitions prediction in dynamic hospital settings, integrating mechanistic epidemiological models into GNNs in a principled manner. Patient-level risk factors learned from dynamic contact networks are jointly leveraged to infer latent epidemiological states, predict state transitions across multiple horizons, and estimate key epidemiological parameters, including transmission and recovery rates. We evaluate the approach on a real-world hospital-onset COVID-19 cohort and two public datasets simulating viral and bacterial HAIs. Across multiple architectures and horizons, EIGNNs achieves AUC-ROC up to 98.46% while providing interpretable, mechanistically consistent insights, offering a transparent tool for infection prevention and control.

title: Effects of Artificial Intelligence Chatbot Interventions on Women during Pregnancy and Postpartum: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
desc: [Healthcare informatics research] Artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots are increasingly used in maternal healthcare to provide real-time, interactive, personalized support. This systematic review and meta-analysis examined the effects of AI chatbot interventions on women during pregnancy and postpartum. PubMed, the Cochrane Library, Embase, the Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature, and the Research Information Sharing System were searched from September 11 to 16, 2025, using the search string "(("Artificial Intelligence"[Mesh] OR "AI"[tiab] OR "Machine Learning"[tiab]) AND ("Chatbot"[tiab] OR "Conversational Agent*"[tiab]) AND ("Pregnancy"[Mesh] OR prenatal[tiab] OR antenatal[tiab] OR postnatal[tiab] OR postpartum[tiab])". Eligible studies were peer-reviewed experimental studies published in English or Korean that evaluated chatbot interventions for women during pregnancy or postpartum. Six studies (four randomized controlled trials and two nonrandomized controlled trials) were included. Intervention themes included gestational diabetes, postpartum depression, well-being, maternal-fetal attachment, aneuploidy testing, and breastfeeding. Individual trials reported improvements in knowledge, self-efficacy, and attachment, as well as reductions in symptoms. The meta-analysis showed no significant effect on depression (estimate = 0.037, p = 0.662) or anxiety (estimate = -0.084, p = 0.279); heterogeneity was low (I² = 0%). AI chatbot interventions show promise for improving maternal knowledge, self-efficacy, and attachment. However, the available evidence does not show consistent reductions in depression or anxiety. Large, rigorously designed studies are needed to refine intervention strategies, ensure equity, and establish a robust basis for integrating these interventions into maternal healthcare systems.

title: AI Treatment Recommendations With Predicted Consequences for Sepsis Fluid and Vasopressor Decisions
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Nanjing University; conditions: Sepsis, Septic Shock; type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 72; status: RECRUITING] When artificial intelligence (AI) recommends a treatment, clinicians must decide whether to follow it. This study tests whether showing the predicted consequences of a recommendation, in addition to the recommendation itself, helps clinicians accept appropriate advice and reject inappropriate advice. We developed a clinician-anchored counterfactual model that compares the on-duty clinician's intravenous fluid and vasopressor plan with alternative plans for patients with sepsis. It predicts the patient's course under each plan and recommends a change only when the predicted benefit holds across several plausible assumptions about unrecorded factors; otherwise it states that the evidence is insufficient to recommend a change. About 72 physicians from two hospitals, stratified by seniority, will review 30 retrospective, de-identified ICU decision points from patients with sepsis. In stage 1, each physician independently specifies fluid and vasopressor doses without any AI information. In stage 2, the same cases are reviewed under three conditions assigned by counterbalanced sequences: the case with the on-duty clinician's plan and no AI (B0); B0 plus the AI recommendation (B1); and B1 plus the predicted consequences of the on-duty and recommended plans (B2). The AI recommendation is identical in B1 and B2. Decision quality is assessed against plans made independently by expert intensivists. No patients are enrolled, and participants' decisions do not affect patient care.

title: A Blockchain-Enabled Federated Ensemble Framework for Privacy-Preserving Mortality Prediction Across Heterogeneous Healthcare Systems

title: Improving Target-Adverse Event Association Prediction via Inverse Node Frequency Transformation to Mitigate Knowledge Graph Topological Bias
desc: Motivation: Identifying significant associations between therapeutic protein targets and adverse events (AEs) is a critical component of drug safety assessment. To accelerate the process, machine learning methods have been developed to predict these associations as edges in network data integrating molecular interactions and other key biomedical knowledge. However, these networks often suffer from topological imbalances where a minority of "hub" nodes determine the predictive signal. This "topological" or "degree bias" can lead to poor performance on novel or understudied targets where safety inference is most needed. Results: We introduce Inverse Node Frequency (INF), a generally applicable node degree-based approach for mitigating topological bias. Employing an enriched biomedical knowledge graph and our own carefully curated target-adverse event associations, we apply INF as a normalisation procedure on a class of graph-derived features called metapaths and evaluate their resulting target-AE association prediction performance. Our results demonstrate that INF significantly improves the true positive rate (TPR/recall) for low-degree targets compared to the untransformed metapath features as well as a popular established normalisation method, while also achieving highly competitive hits@k, a ranking-based metric for knowledge graph-based inference. We also evaluated INF on an external set of target-AE associations never before used for modelling, on which INF also showed superior resilience compared to the two benchmarks.

title: From Sequence Uncertainty to Phenotype Hypotheses: Uncertainty-Conditioned Inference over Biomedical Knowledge Graphs
desc: Genomic foundation models provide variant-level evidence, but connecting that evidence to phenotype hypotheses requires accounting for uncertainty throughout structured reasoning. We introduce an uncertainty-conditioned path-energy framework that converts sequence predictions and calibrated predictive uncertainty into explicit distributions over graph-supported phenotype hypotheses, without patient-level phenotype supervision. An interpretable learned energy scores admissible gene--disease--phenotype routes, query uncertainty controls the target temperature, and path probabilities are aggregated into phenotype hypotheses. This formulation makes evidence quality an explicit determinant of hypothesis breadth while retaining traceable multi-path support. Exact normalization over enumerable candidate sets provides a reference for evaluating a Hastings-corrected learned revision operator. On AlzKB and Hetionet, phenotype-level entropy tracks upstream uncertainty, with Spearman correlations of 0.951 and 0.878, respectively; ablations identify the contribution of uncertainty conditioning. In masked-edge recovery, the model exceeds chance and degree-matched probability-permutation controls. Training the energy under the uncertainty-dependent temperature yields higher held-out recall@10 than training under a constant temperature of comparable magnitude. Under gene hold-out, recall@10 exceeds that of a trained DistMult embedding on 24 of 30 graph masks (0.183 versus 0.123); this difference is attributable mainly to three genes with many variants and is not established for all genes. These results establish an uncertainty-aware interface from genomic predictions to graph-supported phenotype hypotheses that combines interpretable probability allocation with held-out association recovery of explicitly stated scope.

Cloud vs. on-premise large language models for urgent patient-portal message screening: a comparative evaluation
desc: Patient portal messaging carries a substantial share of outpatient communication, and rising message volume has slowed clinical response to urgent concerns embedded in routine traffic. Whether large language models (LLMs) can triage these messages, and whether locally hosted open-weight models can match cloud-hosted ones, remains unclear. We evaluated six LLMs (GPT-4o, GPT-5, GPT-5 Mini, Llama 4 Scout, GPT-OSS 20B, Gemma 3 27B) against a physician reference standard in three cohorts: 500 primary care messages enriched for urgent cases, 503 epilepsy clinic messages from the same health system, and 300 patient-authored messages from public platforms outside it. Under Majority adjudication in primary care, GPT-5 missed no urgent message, and four of six models, including one deployable on-premises, reached sensitivity 0.97 or higher and negative predictive value 0.98 or higher. Rank ordering held across cohorts. Both cloud-hosted and on-premise LLMs can rule out urgent messages with high sensitivity, though specificity remained limited.

title: AI-driven reconstruction of maxillary complete denture bases: a clinical feasibility study.
desc: [Clinical oral investigations] Digital denture workflows remain limited by the inability of intraoral scanners (IOS) to capture functional soft-tissue dynamics and peripheral border molding. This clinical feasibility study evaluated whole-surface geometric reconstruction of maxillary complete denture bases from IOS data using a novel artificial intelligence (AI) model in which peripheral border features were emphasized during training. IOS datasets of the edentulous maxilla and corresponding clinically acceptable dentures from 79 patients were used to train an enhanced PointNet + + model incorporating a border-attention mechanism. The dataset was divided into 57 training, 7 validation, and 15 test cases. Whole-surface point-cloud performance was evaluated in the held-out test set using Density-Aware Chamfer Distance, maximum Hausdorff distance, and multi-threshold precision, recall, and F-scores. Whole-surface registration RMSE was additionally calculated for three randomly selected test-set cases that underwent additive manufacturing and an exploratory clinical try-in. On an independent test set, the mean Chamfer Distance was 2.6 ± 0.1 mm and the maximum Hausdorff distance was 2.4 mm. F-scores increased from 0.8 at a 0.5-mm tolerance to 1.0 at a 2.0-mm tolerance. Whole-surface RMSE values for the three pilot cases ranged from 0.4 to 0.6 mm. The additively manufactured AI denture bases showed promising adaptation and positional stability in this pilot evaluation; however, conventionally fabricated dentures provided superior retention. Within the study's limitations, the AI model showed potential for whole-surface reconstruction of maxillary denture bases from IOS data. However, in the descriptive try-in of three cases, the patients' existing conventional dentures were subjectively more retentive than the additively manufactured AI-generated bases. AI-based denture-base reconstruction from IOS data may contribute to future fully digital workflows. Before clinical implementation, border-specific geometric validation, larger external datasets, and objective measurements of retention, adaptation, and positional stability are required.

title: Educational Methods for Learning Thyroid Ultrasound Interpretation in Medical Students
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Yonsei University; conditions: Thyroid Nodule, Education, Medical, Undergraduate; type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 40; status: ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING] This study compares four educational methods for teaching thyroid ultrasound interpretation to novice learners. Preclinical medical students with no prior training in thyroid ultrasound or the Korean Thyroid Imaging Reporting and Data System (K-TIRADS) are randomly assigned to one of four groups: (A) traditional one-on-one apprenticeship training, (B) self-learning with images labeled only as benign or malignant, (C) self-learning assisted by an artificial intelligence-based computer-aided diagnosis (AI-CAD) system, or (D) self-learning with images structured by K-TIRADS category. The study aims to determine which method most effectively improves diagnostic performance (accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and agreement with expert K-TIRADS assessment), how quickly learners reach a target level of proficiency, whether AI-CAD provides additional educational value for novices, and how each method affects user cognitive load.

title: ClinDataBench: Benchmarking Large Language Model Agents in Clinical Trial Analysis Dataset Construction
desc: A new drug reaches patients only after the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has reviewed its trial evidence, which every application carries as analysis datasets in the Clinical Data Interchange Standards Consortium (CDISC) Analysis Data Model (ADaM) format that programmers derive by hand from raw trial data, a statistical analysis plan (SAP) and dataset specifications. Coding agents built on large language models (LLMs) could take over this work, and a slow-changing industry will adopt them only with evidence of what they get right and wrong. However, work on large language models (LLMs) for CDISC data stops short of evaluating a complete, conformant and reproducible package, and the standard validator checks structure rather than whether each value is derived correctly. We introduce ClinDataBench, built on the public CDISC pilot study: an agent receives 22 Study Data Tabulation Model (SDTM) domains, the statistical analysis plan (SAP) and specifications, and must deliver 13 Analysis Data Model (ADaM) datasets, Define-XML metadata and a program that rebuilds them offline. Agents run in containers whose only network route is their model API, restricting online access to published reference outputs during execution. A host-only evaluator scores conformance under the Pinnacle 21 Community (P21) validator, selected derivations, clean reconstruction and effort separately. We compare three settings: Base, which submits the agent's first package; Self-Refine, which revises it without external validation feedback; and CRITIC, which revises it with the agent's own validator report. In an exploratory pilot with six models, the three closed models and DeepSeek delivered all 13 datasets in every setting and eleven of their twelve packages rebuilt semantically, while two other open-weight models delivered no complete package. Validator findings ranged from 15 to 64 dataset-rule pairs. Four of six CRITIC workflows had usable validator comparisons, and each reduced its finding count. None reduced its failed derivation count. The package with the fewest findings carried none of the 234 efficacy summary records in the form the specifications define, showing that lower validator finding counts do not necessarily indicate more correct derivations.

title: Learning RNA secondary structure from chemical probing with MXfold2
desc: Training RNA secondary structure predictors is limited by scarce reference annotations, even as chemical probing produces abundant nucleotide-level measurements. These measurements inform pairing states without identifying base-pairing partners. Here we extend MXfold2, which combines neural and thermodynamic folding scores, to learn from probing profiles and predict RNA secondary structures from sequence alone. We introduce three training objectives. One learns from probing-assisted target structures. The other two use implicit maximum-likelihood estimation to pass surrogate gradients from reactivity-ranking and likelihood losses through discrete folding. Simulations, RNAgym measurements and external structural tests show improved chemical agreement and gains in exact base-pair prediction when chemical supervision is combined with structural pretraining and replay. Probing profiles can thus broaden the range of RNAs that inform sequence-only structure prediction, including RNA populations with few complete structure annotations.

title: Statistical, Machine Learning and Deep Learning Methods for Missing Covariates: An Empirical Evaluation with Applications to Alzheimer's Disease Research
desc: Missing data are common in biomedical research, particularly when biomarkers are costly or require invasive procedures to obtain, such as cerebrospinal fluid measures in Alzheimer's disease. Although a wide range of missing data methods exists, from traditional statistical approaches to modern machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) algorithms, their comparative performance under different missingness mechanisms remains insufficiently understood. In this study, we provide an empirical evaluation of eight methods for handling missing covariates, including complete-case analysis, multiple imputation, ML-based techniques, and DL frameworks such as multilayer perceptrons, variational autoencoders, and generative adversarial networks. We summarize their conceptual foundations, practical implementation considerations, strengths, and limitations. Through extensive simulations, we assess estimation bias, efficiency, standard error accuracy, confidence interval coverage, and computational burden across different missingness mechanisms and proportions. An application to the Vanderbilt Memory and Aging Project further illustrates the implications of different methods for regression analysis in a real-world biomedical setting. Finally, we provide practical recommendations for method selection and highlight remaining challenges that warrant future investigation.

Shape-informed cardiac mechanics surrogates in data-scarce regimes via geometric encoding and generative augmentation
desc: High-fidelity computational models of cardiac mechanics provide mechanistic insight into the heart function but are computationally prohibitive for routine clinical use. Surrogate models can accelerate simulations, but generalization across diverse anatomies is challenging, particularly in data-scarce settings. We propose a two-step framework that decouples geometric representation from learning the physics response, to enable shape-informed surrogate modeling under data-scarce conditions. First, a shape model learns a compact latent representation of left ventricular geometries. The learned latent space effectively encodes anatomies and enables synthetic geometries generation for data augmentation. Second, a neural field-based surrogate model, conditioned on this geometric encoding, is trained to predict ventricular displacement under external loading. The proposed architecture performs positional encoding by using universal ventricular coordinates, which improves generalization across diverse anatomies. Geometric variability is encoded using two alternative strategies, which are systematically compared: a PCA-based approach suitable for working with point cloud representations of geometries, and a DeepSDF-based implicit neural representation learned directly from point clouds. Overall, our results, obtained on idealized and patient-specific datasets, show that the proposed approaches allow for accurate predictions and generalization to unseen geometries, and robustness to noisy or sparsely sampled inputs.

title: Expert-level localization of fine-grained cardiac structures across the transthoracic echocardiogram.
source: PubMed · medRxiv : the preprint server for health sciences
desc: [medRxiv : the preprint server for health sciences] 1.Artificial intelligence models for echocardiography interpret studies without identifying the structures that support their outputs. We show that this spatial grounding does not emerge from the pretraining of current vision-language models. General-purpose and medical vision-language models and an open-vocabulary detector recalled 3% or fewer of cardiac structures and scored below a box that never sees the image. EchoLens, a detector trained on 5,912 expert-annotated structures and 4,219 Doppler signals from 136 patients, recalled 87% and localized structures as reliably as a blinded expert reader (box centre within the reference in 95.7% and 95.3% of cases). It covers 21 structures across 11 transthoracic views and 11 spectral Doppler signal types. In external data, two physicians judged 81- 92% of its detections correct across all 11 views, and it identified the Doppler signal type in 83% of frames. EchoLens provides the spatial layer that grounded echocardiographic interpretation requires.

title: AI-powered Childbirth Preparation Training
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Pamukkale University; conditions: Increase in Natural Birth Belief and Reduction in Fear of Childbirth, Childbirth-related Anxiety, and Cesarean Deliveries Through AI; type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 44; status: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] This randomized controlled study aims to evaluate the effect of an artificial intelligence (AI)-supported mobile childbirth preparation program on birth beliefs, childbirth-related worries, fear of childbirth, and mode of delivery in primigravid women. High rates of planned cesarean section are associated with fear of childbirth, negative birth beliefs, and insufficient prenatal preparation. This study investigates whether a personalized, AI-supported digital education model can improve psychological outcomes and reduce planned cesarean preference. Study Design Single-blind, pretest-posttest randomized controlled trial. Participants (primigravid women at 28-32 weeks of gestation) will be randomly assigned to: Intervention Group: AI-supported mobile childbirth preparation education Control Group: Standard antenatal care only Primary outcomes include changes in birth beliefs, childbirth-related worries, and fear of childbirth. Secondary outcome is mode of delivery (vaginal birth vs. planned cesarean). Eligibility Criteria (Key Inclusion) Age ≥18 years Primigravid 28-32 weeks of gestation No high-risk pregnancy Access to a mobile device Ethical Approval Ethical approval has been obtained from the Pamukkale University Non-Interventional Clinical Research Ethics Committee (29 July 2025, No: 14).

title: Patient- and Family-Expressed Needs and Burdens in Kidney-Related Online Discussions in Taiwan: Large Language Model-Based Analysis Across Clinical Contexts
desc: Introduction: What people with kidney concerns or disease and their families struggle with between visits may not surface in clinic. We mapped the needs and burdens they express online by clinical context and author. Methods: A large language model read all 22,170 posts reached by a chronic kidney disease tag or kidney lexicon on a Taiwanese forum and 3 ask-a-physician services (1995-2026), applying a companion friction framework with kidney-specific fields, author (patient or family) and clinical context. A second vendor re-read 11,010 posts; 2 physicians labelled relevance, author and context in 200. Results: Among 6,023 kidney-related posts, the reproducibly measured fields most often voiced on the forum were information needs (79%), emotional burden (48%), system navigation (34%) and worry about progression (24%). After abnormal tests, 54%-56% of posts quoted a laboratory value, nearly always with a question or stated uncertainty; renal-diet burden peaked with diagnosed disease; caregiver burden rose to 29% of dialysis-or-transplantation forum posts. Family-written posts more often voiced navigation difficulty and caregiver burden. Most fields agreed with the second vendor (kappa 0.65-0.98). On the model's labels, family members wrote 25% of forum posts about kidney concerns and 74% about dialysis or transplantation; on a 139-post sample, physicians' labels gave 47%-48% for dialysis or transplantation (model 71%). Conclusion: Kidney-related posts carry context-specific information needs and emotional and practical burdens, many voiced by relatives. They suggest candidate responses (test-result explanation, diet support, family-directed information and support) that need evaluation. Keywords: chronic kidney disease; dialysis; patient experience; caregivers; social media; large language models

title: Contactless Estimation of Respiratory Frequency Using 3D-CNN on Thermal Images
desc: Monitoring physiological parameters such as respiratory rate ($f_R$) is essential for diagnosing and managing various pathological conditions. Thermal imaging offers a promising contactless alternative to traditional methods, which often rely on partially invasive sensors or obtrusive wearable systems. However, existing approaches for $f_R$ estimation from thermal signals typically require extensive pre-processing and manual or semi-automatic region-of-interest (ROI) tracking, limiting their practical applicability. This study proposes a deep learning-based method for estimating $f_R$ directly from thermal videos, eliminating the need for complex pre-processing and ROI tracking. A 3D Convolutional Neural Network (3D-CNN) is developed to operate on raw thermal video data. To address challenges related to small datasets, the model is trained using data augmentation and transfer learning from synthetic datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves a validation $R^2$ score of approximately 0.61 on both pre-processed and raw thermal videos. By simplifying the workflow, this method holds promise for enhancing the feasibility of thermal imaging in real-world applications, such as remote healthcare and driver monitoring in automotive applications.

Research progress and prospects of cochlear implant technology.
desc: [Frontiers in neuroscience] Traditional cochlear implant systems depend on external devices and face challenges related to convenience, esthetics, and auditory performance in complex soundscapes. Recently, research has shifted from "functional substitution" to "functional enhancement" and "biological fusion." However, most emerging approaches remain in the preclinical, prototype verification, or early clinical stages, lacking substantial evidence of clinical benefits. This narrative review examines research progress across five key dimensions of cochlear implants: The electrode interface has advanced from passive implants to dynamic, adaptive, and biologically active intelligent interfaces. Signal processing strategies are moving toward intelligence and physiological adaptation, with deep learning primarily used for noise suppression and coding optimization; however, clinical application is limited by real-time performance and individual variability. Bionic sensing aims to replicate the energy conversion mechanism between hair cells and the basement membrane at the signal source, currently focusing on laboratory prototypes. Optogenetics-driven optical regulation offers high spatial selectivity but remains in the early preclinical stage. The development of fully implanted systems emphasizes internal energy supply, ultra-low power consumption processing, and system integration, marking a significant engineering direction for making devices "invisible." Each section of this article critically evaluates evidence maturity and transformation barriers, highlighting common challenges such as long-term biological stability, safety, energy consumption, and regulatory verification that must be addressed before large-scale clinical application. Future advancements will require collaboration among materials science, neuroscience, microelectronics, and artificial intelligence to create a two-way high-fidelity interface. The ultimate goal is not only to restore hearing but also to reconstruct a more natural auditory perception.

title: Effects of AI-Assisted Clinical Recommendations on Dental Students' Endodontic Antibiotic Prescribing Decisions
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Tolga Mavigöz; conditions: Antibiotic Prescribing Decision-Making; type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 328; status: COMPLETED] This study evaluated how artificial intelligence (AI)-formatted clinical recommendations influence dental students' decisions about prescribing systemic antibiotics in endodontic cases. In this randomized, three-arm, parallel-group, online experimental study, third-, fourth-, and fifth-year dental students in Türkiye were assigned to one of three conditions: a Control group receiving no AI recommendations, a Guideline-concordant AI group receiving recommendations consistent with established clinical guidance, or a Mixed-accuracy AI group receiving recommendations with varying levels of accuracy. Participants evaluated ten hypothetical endodontic clinical scenarios and decided whether systemic antibiotic treatment was indicated. The primary outcome was the accuracy of antibiotic prescribing decisions compared with predefined reference decisions. Secondary outcomes included confidence in clinical decisions, trust in AI recommendations, agreement with recommendations, identification of potentially incorrect information, and inappropriate antibiotic prescribing patterns. Data were collected between July 1 and July 6, 2026. A total of 328 participants were randomized, 318 met the eligibility criteria, and 271 completed all ten primary decision questions.

title: Simulation and temporal validation of ICU trajectories after stroke: patient condition, transfer readiness and actual ICU exit
desc: Objective: To describe how intensive care unit (ICU) time is composed after stroke, and to test whether simulating patient condition, transfer readiness and ICU exit separately predicts as accurately as direct models. Materials and Methods: In 6,366 ICU stays for stroke in MIMIC IV, hourly readiness criteria divided ICU hours into organ support needs, stroke specific needs, and time not explained by these needs. An hourly simulator was built on stays up to 2016, frozen, and validated on 2017 to 2019 (n=1,714) and 2020 onwards (n=1,521). The primary measure was the 24 hour alive exit Brier score versus the strongest direct model (gradient boosting). Results: Unexplained time was 34.1% of hours in standard ICUs and 87.6% in neuro intermediate units. 37.8% of stays lost readiness for [≥]6 consecutive hours after first confirmation. The simulator and gradient boosting were indistinguishable (Brier 0.1238 vs 0.1245; difference -0.0007, 95% CI -0.0030 to 0.0016). The simulator was better calibrated at 48 and 72 hours but discriminated less well (C statistic 0.71 vs 0.74 to 0.75). All models overpredicted exit after 2016; the error lay mainly after readiness (median 40 hours simulated vs 68 observed). Discussion: Readiness was not a single event: patients often lost and regained it, and many stayed long after meeting it, especially in neuro intermediate units, which exist for monitoring. Separate modelling did not improve accuracy but placed the post 2016 error after readiness, as the unit mix changed. Conclusion: The simulator matched the strongest direct model while also generating complete trajectories. It needs external validation before any clinical use.

title: A Statistical Framework for Training Data Auditing of Large Language Models
desc: Training-data auditing asks whether data of interest were used to train a large language model (LLM), a question central to privacy auditing, copyright protection, and benchmark-contamination detection. These concerns are particularly relevant to the use of copyrighted books and scientific papers in pre-training, as well as synthetic text and medical question-answer records in fine-tuning. In practice, training membership signals may be concentrated in only a few passages of a long document, making it important to aggregate evidence within each document without diluting these localized signals. Beyond individual documents, auditing a target collection requires an overall assessment based on the document-level evidence. In this paper, we propose a unified statistical framework for document-level membership inference, target-collection global auditing, and suspicious-subset identification. We integrate complementary chunk-level membership evidence with Cauchy combination to construct document scores for document-level membership inference. The document scores and their calibrated p-values further enable an overall assessment of training-data collection use and the identification of suspicious documents through multiple testing. Under the stated exchangeability conditions, we establish finite-sample validity of document-level p-values, type-I error control for global auditing, and false discovery rate control for subset identification. Case studies on BookTection, Pile-arXiv, Cosmopedia, and HealthCareMagic demonstrate the effectiveness and reliability of the proposed framework in auditing pre-training and fine-tuning data.
