Artificial intelligence in nursing education: A bibliometric and visualized analysis of screened literature (2022-2026).
desc: [Nurse education in practice] Based on a systematically screened corpus of literature, this bibliometric study aims to map the research landscape and hotspots of artificial intelligence (AI) in nursing education from 2022 to 2026 and provide evidence-based guidance for future research and educational practice. The rapid integration of AI and digital transformation is fundamentally reshaping nursing education, yet a comprehensive, up-to-date overview of its research landscape remains lacking. Bibliometric and content analysis. Publications were retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection (January 2022-June 2026). Using CiteSpace 6.4.R1, co-occurrence, cluster, burst and timeline analyses were performed to visualize the knowledge structure and identify emerging research frontiers. A total of 409 publications were included, with output surging in 2025 and most papers appearing in JCR Q1/Q2 journals. The United States, China and Türkiye led output, but cross-national and cross-institutional collaboration remained sparse. Three predominant research clusters were identified: applications of AI in nursing education, attitudes and readiness of nursing students and educators toward AI and capacity building for AI implementation. The field is expanding rapidly yet remains fragmented and exploratory. Three priorities are proposed: guiding technology adoption by the competencies curricula intend to develop rather than technological novelty; treating readiness as a dynamic construct and shifting assessment toward process-oriented evidence; and positioning capacity building-tiered AI literacy and faculty development, curriculum integration and ethical and policy-oriented governance-as a safeguard for sustainable AI integration. Strengthening international collaboration will underpin these priorities.

title: Using a large language model as the primary coder in health content analysis: a verification framework, per-variable reliability and proposed reporting items.
desc: Objective: To describe and evaluate a framework for using a large language model (LLM) as the primary coder in health content analysis, and to propose reporting items for LLM assisted studies, because no reporting standard exists. Methods: An LLM coded 6,982 Instagram and TikTok posts using a human written, human calibrated instrument. The framework has six components: human authorship of the instrument; two round human calibration; source discipline; quote anchored coding; verification in a representative and an outcome enriched sample, blinded in both directions; and per variable reliability reporting against a prespecified threshold, with the consequence of failure fixed in advance. Agreement was measured with Gwets AC1, prespecified because the outcome distribution was heavily skewed. Results: Agreement between the two human coders on the primary outcome rose from AC1 0.456 to 0.977 after two ambiguous rules were rewritten. LLM human agreement was 0.847 in the representative sample (N = 150) and 0.868 in the enriched sample (N = 50). Five of eight conditional variables fell below the 0.80 threshold and became exploratory: variables asking whether a defined textual feature was present met it, whereas those requiring graded judgement did not. The human coder identified misinformation more often than the LLM, so prevalence estimates are likely underestimates. Agreement on female targeting was lower for self-identified ethnic minority creators (0.744 versus 0.902). Conclusion: LLM coding cannot be computationally reproduced, so its reliability must be shown empirically: per variable agreement with independent human coding, the direction of remaining error, and a prespecified response to shortfall. The authors propose 18 reporting items for LLM assisted content analysis.

title: Physics-Informed Deep Learning for Shear Wave Speed Estimation in MR Elastography
desc: Objective: Magnetic Resonance Elastography (MRE) is a non-invasive imaging technique for mapping biomechanical properties of in vivo tissue, including shear wave speed (SWS), but involves intrinsically slow data acquisition and an ill-posed wave inversion. Instead of relying on handcrafted image priors, we propose a data-driven approach jointly combining image reconstruction and MRE inversion for robust SWS estimation from undersampled k-space data. Methods: Our physics-informed reconstruction framework comprises two blocks: a model-based neural network (NN)-regularized reconstruction module and a phase-gradient inversion (k-MDEV) calculating SWS from the reconstructed images. Concatenating both blocks yields an end-to-end trainable method to estimate SWS directly from measured k-space data. We evaluated the method on retrospectively highly undersampled brain MRE data and compared it to a total variation (TV) minimization-based approach. We assessed the impact of end-to-end training (qualitative images and SWS maps as targets) versus pre-training (qualitative images as targets) and applied the method also to in vivo data. Results: Our approach significantly reduces NRMSE by 30% compared to TV. End-to-end training improves SWS estimation over separate image reconstruction and SWS calculation. Conclusion: Accurate SWS quantification is possible at acceleration factors up to 19. Our method significantly outperforms TV, highlighting the need for data-driven regularization in this challenging MR problem. Further, our approach successfully generalizes to in vivo data. Significance: We present the first end-to-end trainable MRE reconstruction method for estimating SWS maps directly from k-space. NN-based reconstruction can enable rapid stiffness mapping for dynamic studies, functional imaging, and real-time clinical feedback.

title: Rollout models of human planning with exact action probabilities.
desc: [PLoS computational biology] One proposed mechanism for human planning is the mental simulation, or "rollout," of potential action sequences to evaluate future outcomes. While rollout-based models have seen great success in artificial intelligence, cognitive models that describe how people use rollouts remain scarce, in part because they are difficult to fit to behavioral data. Existing methods rely on computationally intensive simulations that result in approximate, noisy estimates of latent planning parameters. We introduce ROSETTE (Rollouts with Stochastic Early Termination and Tractable Estimation), a rollout-based model for finite goal-directed tasks with absorbing goals that provides analytically tractable, simulation-free model fitting. ROSETTE treats planning as a sequence of mental simulations formalized as an absorbing Markov chain. The model deterministically accumulates analytically computed expected rollout evidence and performs a variable number of policy-update cycles. We fit ROSETTE to data from human participants in two multi-step planning tasks and found that it well accounted for a rich set of summary statistics of behavior. By making this specific class of absorbing-goal rollout models tractable, our framework provides a testable account of how people may simulate and evaluate possible futures.

title: Preferences for Accessible Health Information Among Deaf, Blind, and DeafBlind Adults: A Descriptive Qualitative Study
desc: Overview. People with sensory disabilities (e.g., deaf or hard-of-hearing [DHH], blind/low vision [BLV], and DeafBlind) encounter difficulties when accessing health information. These barriers impede people with sensory disabilities in obtaining, understanding, and using health information. This study aimed to identify barriers, facilitators, and preferred formats for health information to inform inclusive health communication, while addressing the variety of accessibility needs across people who are DHH, BLV, and DeafBlind. Methods. We conducted a qualitative study using eight focus groups and eleven individual interviews with adults with different types of sensory disabilities. Interviews were conducted directly in English or American Sign Language, and recordings were professionally transcribed. Discussions explored experiences accessing health information, information source preferences, accessibility barriers, and reactions to different formats. Transcripts were coded using a hybrid thematic analysis process. Themes were generated through team discussions, code synthesis, and community partner feedback. Results. We developed three themes summarizing user-centered perspectives for designing consumer health information resources. Participants obtained health information from various sources including clinicians, family, friends, internet searches, and ChatGPT. Barriers included information overload, medical jargon, inaccessible website design, and communication breakdowns with clinicians. Preferences for health information formats differed across disability groups. Key recommendations included simplified language, structured layouts, and compatibility with assistive technologies (e.g., screen readers). Conclusion. Despite varying accessibility needs across disabilities, participants agreed health information must be delivered through multiple accessible formats to meet diverse sensory needs. These findings are being used to develop health promotion checklists to enhance accessibility for people with sensory disabilities.

title: Explainability of genotype embedding models through observed cohort paths
desc: Deep learning models that combine genotypes with neuroimaging predict neurological diseases more accurately than either modality alone. Their clinical use, however, requires identifying which genetic variants a prediction is based on. Path-based attribution methods like Integrated Gradients address this by integrating the model's gradient from a baseline to the input. These methods assume the model accepts any point along that path as a valid input. Genotype models violate this assumption. They map the three discrete allele dosages \{0,1,2\} to vectors through a learned embedding defined only at those values, so a straight line passes through fractional genotypes at which no embedding, and therefore no gradient, exists. Attribution must therefore proceed in embedding space where the choice of path can affect the resulting attribution. We show that the commonly used per-variant estimator does not generally satisfy completeness. Additive separability guarantees completeness for this estimator, but interactions between variants generally break that property. Instead, we integrate along piecewise-linear embedding-space paths connecting genotype waypoints observed in the training cohort. Each path satisfies completeness in the continuum although the interiors of its segments are not necessarily observed. Our method improves faithfulness over Integrated Gradients and discretized Integrated Gradients under both perturbation protocols, achieves the strongest results for Parkinson's disease classification under support-preserving perturbations, and is competitive with a support-background Shapley baseline under per-variant perturbations. It also shows higher seed stability and better recovery of planted non-additive effects in a synthetic benchmark.

title: Unsupervised Selective Labeling for Semi-Supervised Aerial Imagery Recognition.
desc: [Ecology and evolution] Traditional aerial wildlife monitoring surveys rely on rapid visual identification and counting by expert biologists from moving aircraft. Modern camera systems mounted on survey aircraft are now being deployed to collect large datasets of imagery that provide a persistent, reusable snapshot of wildlife populations. Manual analysis of these extensive datasets can overwhelm the staffing of natural resource agencies, especially for large-scale surveys. Deep learning systems are being investigated as a potential solution to automate analysis, but significant human effort is still required to curate a labeled dataset for model training. To address this challenge, we propose Semi-Supervised Aerial Imagery Recognition (referred to as SSAR), a framework that minimizes annotation effort while maintaining classification performance. The key of SSAR is to select the best subset of images for annotation while leveraging the hidden information from the remaining unlabeled data. Concretely, SSAR integrates three components: (1) unsupervised feature learning tailored to aerial imagery to capture ecologically meaningful visual patterns, (2) unsupervised selective labeling that prioritizes representative and diverse images for annotation, and (3) semi-supervised classification that incorporates the remaining unlabeled images during training. We evaluate SSAR on wildlife recognition case studies using object-centric image crops from high-resolution aerial imagery collected over the United States Atlantic Outer Continental Shelf (OCS) and the Great Lakes region, comprising 57,265 images across 11 coarse categories. Using only 6.4% labeled data, SSAR matches the fully supervised macro accuracy of 85.0% achieved with 100% labeled data and further surpasses it by reaching 86.8% with 12.8% labeled data. These results demonstrate that SSAR enables accurate and scalable aerial wildlife recognition with an order-of-magnitude reduction in manual annotation.

title: REMI: A Free Tool for Truncated Proximity Searching in PubMed
desc: Background: PubMed is the most comprehensive freely available database for medical and health sciences publications, making it an essential platform for literature searching in budget-constrained settings (e.g. non-academic hospitals). However, unlike subscription platforms (e.g. Ovid MEDLINE), it cannot combine truncation with proximity operators. Searchers must therefore either enumerate every word form manually, risking missed variants, or fall back on Boolean AND, which retrieves many irrelevant records. We developed REMI (Related Expression Machine Identification), a free, open-source web application which emulates truncated proximity searching in PubMed. Case Presentation: REMI was developed at Maastricht University Library. Through the NCBI E-utilities, it identifies the variants of truncated terms that occur in PubMed records. An iterative exclusion procedure, which reruns the search for each concept while excluding that concept's variants already found, surfaces progressively rarer forms. Users select relevant variants from frequency-ranked lists, and REMI combines them into native PubMed proximity clauses that can be documented, peer reviewed, and rerun without REMI. Performance of REMI was evaluated by comparison to four Ovid MEDLINE search strategies from published reviews. REMI's proximity search was able to identify all included articles found with the original Ovid MEDLINE query. Conclusions: REMI makes truncated proximity searching available in PubMed while keeping searches transparent, reliable, and reproducible, which particularly benefits searchers without access to subscription platforms. Because variant discovery is a sampling procedure, completeness is not guaranteed, and long searches require variant selection. Other libraries can use, host, or adapt the tool, however, native support in PubMed would remain the preferable solution.

title: QUBO-based feature selection for MRI undersampling pattern design
desc: We formulate undersampling mask design for Cartesian magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) as a feature subset selection problem. Each sampling line is represented by a binary feature indicating whether it is included in each candidate mask. Using candidate masks and their training-set evaluations, we estimate mutual information (MI) and conditional mutual information (CMI). These estimates and a sampling-count penalty define a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) model. The model is solved using simulated annealing and quantum annealing to determine a feature subset and its corresponding sampling mask. We assess the selected subsets on the test set through zero-filled reconstruction in Fourier undersampling simulations using fastMRI knee magnitude reference images, with patient-disjoint training and test sets. At all six tested target sampling rates from 15% to 40%, the resulting reconstructions have lower mean root mean square error than those obtained with four conventional sampling methods. They also have higher mean structural similarity than those obtained using univariate mutual-information ranking at all tested rates. These results support information-theoretic feature selection as an approach to MRI undersampling mask design under the tested zero-filled simulation settings.

title: Building an Auditable Reference Standard for Clinical Information Extraction from Transesophageal Echocardiography Reports
desc: Objectives To develop an auditable, two-institution reference standard for intraoperative transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) reports and evaluate whether reviewer disagreement identifies limitations in the underlying clinical information model. Materials and Methods We selected 300 reports (150 per institution) from 925 at the University of Pennsylvania and University of Washington using random sampling and enrichment for challenging documentation. Four trained abstractors applied a shared 39-variable V1 codebook. Independent paired comparisons included 297 reports; three historical reports contributed only to the final reference standard. Categorical agreement used exact agreement and unweighted Cohen's {kappa}; numeric left-ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) used exact agreement and mean absolute differences. Disagreements underwent structured expert adjudication and reason classification. Additional analyses assessed reviewer-pair, sampling-stratified, and population-weighted agreement. Results Among 11,583 formal reviewer-comparison cells, 10,293 (88.9%) were resolved by reviewer agreement and 1,290 (11.1%) required targeted expert adjudication (1,289 tasks). Codebook/schema ambiguity (40.8%) and interpretation/classification differences (25.2%) together accounted for 66.0% of targeted tasks. Adjudication was concentrated in aortic dissection, valve type, and post-intervention findings. Categorical {kappa} ranged from 0.364 to 0.960 and was inversely correlated with targeted-adjudication burden (Spearman {rho}=-0.884; 95% CI, -0.955 to -0.734). Sampling-weighted {kappa} changed by no more than 0.05 for 32 of 35 categorical variables. Discussion Structured adjudication identified recurring schema and interpretation challenges beyond individual abstraction errors, providing specific targets for information-model refinement. Conclusion As NLP and LLM-based abstraction tools move toward clinical use, the reference standards used to evaluate them require comparably rigorous development, adjudication, and independent validation.

title: Empirical Variational Bayes Factorization for Longitudinal Matrix Data
desc: Collecting high-dimensional data over time for multiple individuals is increasingly common in biomedical research, particularly in studies of disease progression or molecular time-course experiments. Often data are missing or the timepoints are irregularly spaced across individuals. There is a lack of flexible methodology to explore latent patterns of change over time and account for missing data. We propose an empirical variational Bayes (EVB) approach to factorize high-dimensional longitudinal data, in which the underlying factors have temporal correlation over time. The EVB approach is computationally efficient and accommodates flexible covariance structures over time with automatic determination of all hyper-parameters (including the underlying rank, i.e., number of factors). Simulations demonstrate that the approach captures the underlying signal more precisely than other strategies, and performs well with respect to missing data imputation under different scenarios. An application to a gene time-course data for multiple sclerosis treatment provides a factorization with interpretable components over time and improved imputation accuracy for missing data.

title: Automated Screening for Generalized Anxiety Disorder Using Voice Analysis and Machine Learning
desc: This study evaluated machine learning models for screening elevated generalized anxiety symptoms from remotely collected neutral read speech in 1,788 adults from Botswana, Ghana, Nigeria, and Tanzania. Elevated symptoms were defined by Generalized Anxiety Disorder 7-item (GAD-7) questionnaire scores [≥] 5. Nine classifiers were assessed across nine scenarios defined by speech-task configuration (short sentence, long passage, or both tasks) and sex stratification under participant-separated, repeated nested cross-validation (CV). Acoustic-only models used the extended Geneva Minimalistic Acoustic Parameter Set, and context-augmented models added age, self-reported health, and sex where applicable. With feature selection, the highest mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUCROC) was 0.594 for acoustic-only models and 0.699 for context-augmented models, the latter in the female-only combined-task scenario. Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) identified fundamental frequency descriptors as prominent acoustic predictors, while health status and age were the leading predictors in context-augmented models. Performance varied across scenarios, and feature selection provided no consistent benefit. Secondary regression poorly estimated continuous symptom severity. These findings indicate limited discrimination from neutral speech acoustics alone and improved performance with participant context, warranting external validation.

title: When Foundation Models Disagree: Representational Heterogeneity for Calibrated Uncertainty in Whole-Slide Image Classification
desc: Pathology foundation models supply strong representations for whole-slide image classification, yet the confidence attached to their predictions remains hard to trust. Prevailing uncertainty estimators act within a single feature space and thereby overlook the uncertainty that the choice of foundation-model representation itself induces. This work introduces CALIFUSE, a calibration-oriented framework that fuses several pathology foundation models for the specific purpose of uncertainty estimation. Departing from accuracy-driven fusion, CALIFUSE reads representational heterogeneity across encoders as an explicit confidence cue. Slide-level decision consensus is coupled with chunk-level evidence agreement quantified through Jensen-Shannon divergence, so that both prediction stability and fine-grained evidence consistency inform the estimate. Foundation-model encoders stay frozen. A task-specific nnMIL classifier is still trained for each FM; CALIFUSE then estimates confidence at inference without training an extra fusion module. Evaluated on seven WSI classification tasks under several foundation-model combinations, the framework sharpens calibration, misclassification detection, and selective prediction relative to both the strongest single-encoder baseline and naive ensemble averaging, all while preserving competitive balanced accuracy.

title: Development and Validation of MetaVidence: A No-Code Application for Accessible and Reproducible Meta-analysis
desc: BACKGROUND: Meta-analyses are central to evidence-based medicine, but the R packages that implement current methods require programming skills, and most graphical tools cover only a single study design. Here, we aimed to develop and validate a free no-code application that performs the main forms of meta-analysis within a single interface. METHODS: We developed MetaVidence as a Shiny application built on the meta, metafor, netmeta and lme4 packages, which runs in the browser through WebAssembly and is also available as an R package. Agreement with direct package calls was evaluated across effect measures, models, estimators and secondary analyses, and 12 published meta-analyses were reconstructed. Usability was assessed with the System Usability Scale among researchers who had previously conducted a meta-analysis. RESULTS: MetaVidence performs pairwise, single-arm, pre-calculated, network and diagnostic test accuracy meta-analysis through a three-step workflow of data verification, model specification and results. In three of the five families, multiple outcomes can be analyzed in a single run with the same settings, and every analysis reports the parameters that should be described in the methods section. A total of 6,321 validation checks were performed, and the maximum absolute difference in the reference-dataset comparisons was 3.9x10^(-16). The diagnostic module reproduced the anti-CCP example of the Cochrane Handbook to within 0.0002, and all 12 published meta-analyses were reproduced within half of the last reported digit. Fifty-nine researchers rated MetaVidence with a mean System Usability Scale score of 82.8 (95% CI 76.2-89.5). CONCLUSIONS: MetaVidence integrates the main forms of meta-analysis into a single validated interface that does not require programming. These findings support its use as an accessible and reproducible resource for evidence synthesis, particularly for researchers without programming skills or statistical support.

title: Disentangling Monitor Hardware Artifacts and Smoothing Lag for Shift-Robust Intraoperative EEG and Hemodynamic Risk Calibration
desc: Commercial intraoperative electroencephalography (EEG) and blood pressure monitors introduce cyclic impedance pulses, smoothing delays, direct-current (DC) drift, and cuff holds that confound risk forecasting and uncertainty calibration. We developed a causal signal-conditioning and shift-robust conformal calibration framework across 5,439 public anesthesia procedures. Streaming filters blank 10.13-min 64-Hz impedance checks, apply unclipped post-notch conditioning, separate 63-s suppression-ratio lag, and distinguish three-channel cuff inflations from dropouts across propofol-remifentanil total intravenous anesthesia (TIVA; N = 3,214), volatile anesthesia (N = 2,046), European endoscopy sedation (N = 171), and DC-coupled surgery (N = 8). De-impedanced cortical tree ensembles were compared against deep sequence models, paired with patient-cluster Subgroup-Covariate-Weighted Conformal Risk Control (CRC) and lag-buffered online Conformal Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) tracking. Pre-filter blanking removed 97.90% and 97.60% of false flatline conflicts while preserving 99.23% and 98.96% of deep suppression. On unseen TIVA surgeries (N = 525), cortical features achieved area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) 0.3135 (1.94% prevalence) and 0.1627 (0.82% lag-free prevalence), with no detectable difference from deep encoders (p >= 0.36) and no cortical gain for hypotension (0.3432 vs. 0.3437, p = 0.784). Zero-retraining volatile transfer (N = 1,048) showed no detectable difference from an end-tidal gas oracle on lag-free suppression (0.0820 vs. 0.0736, p = 0.472). Subgroup-Covariate-Weighted CRC bounded all 70 TIVA shift cells at <= 4.38% (alpha = 5.0%) in 66.32 ms per 30-s epoch. Causal artifact disentangling and shift-aware conformal calibration support reliable real-time intraoperative risk bounds within explicit physiological observability limits.

title: PAIR-MED: Policy-reward Alternation for Iterative Refinement in Multilingual Medical Reasoning
desc: Large language models demonstrate strong medical question-answering capabilities, yet reasoning performance remains uneven across languages. Process reward models (PRMs) provide step-level feedback for improving reasoning, but a fixed PRM may become increasingly misaligned with the trajectory distribution of an evolving policy during reinforcement learning, thereby reducing the reliability of its supervision. We propose a policy--reward alternating training framework that jointly adapts a medical PRM and optimizes a multilingual reasoning policy. Following supervised initialization, the current policy generates multilingual trajectories to update the PRM, which then provides process-level rewards for the next policy update. Medical step supervision maintains the PRM's medical foundation, while process, outcome, and language-related rewards guide policy learning. We develop multilingual medical PRMs (PAIR-PRM) and reasoning models (PAIR-MED) at 8B and 9B scales across 12 languages. On the medical subsets of Global-MMLU and MMLU-ProX, our models improve average accuracy by 3.01--7.47% over their corresponding Qwen backbones. On CUREMED-BENCH, PAIR-MED-9B improves the joint language consistency and logical accuracy metric by 12.88% and 7.45% over baselines for in-domain and out-of-domain languages. Further analyses examine PRM adaptation, multilingual reasoning quality, and the contributions of individual training components.
